studies.Screening Record ID: 42404163|Ultra-processed food intake|Kidney and renal pelvis cancer
studies.Population: NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study participants with no cancer history at baseline
studies.Ethnicity Basis: Default: no protocol-mapped specific country or population was established
studies.Ethnicity Supporting Text: Among 480,347 participants, the median (interquartile range [IQR]) age was 62.6 (57.7-66.6), 59.6% (n = 286,150) were male, 91.3% (n = 438,355) were White.
studies.Reference: Ultra-processed food intake and risk of renal cell carcinoma in the NIH-AARP Diet and health study: a prospective cohort analysis.
studies.Authors: Burns KF, Purdue MP, Khandpur N, Martinez-Steele E, Sinha R, Hong HG, Loftfield E
studies.comparison_type: Q4 versus Q1 of ultra-processed food intake
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Diet was self-reported using a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ). FFQ items were assigned to Nova classifications to determine UPF intake (grams per day per 1000 kcal).

sample_size.excerpt: Among 480,347 participants, the median (interquartile range [IQR]) age was 62.6 (57.7-66.6), 59.6% (n = 286,150) were male, 91.3% (n = 438,355) were White.

cases.excerpt: There were 3330 RCC diagnoses over follow-up, of which 1216 were cc-RCC.

effect_size.excerpt: Higher UPF intake was associated with higher RCC [HR (95% CI)<sub>Q4 vs Q1</sub> = 1.16 (1.05-1.29), p-trend = 0.0006] and cc-RCC risk [1.38 (1.17-1.62), p-trend <0.0001]. Associations remained but were attenuated when adjusting for body mass index (BMI), diet quality, or hypertension status.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Higher UPF intake was associated with higher RCC [HR (95% CI)<sub>Q4 vs Q1</sub> = 1.16 (1.05-1.29), p-trend = 0.0006] and cc-RCC risk [1.38 (1.17-1.62), p-trend <0.0001].

design.excerpt: In the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study, a US prospective cohort, participants with no cancer history at baseline (October 1995-May 1996) were followed until the date of first cancer diagnosis, death, or end of follow-up (December 31, 2018).

timing.excerpt: In the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study, a US prospective cohort, participants with no cancer history at baseline (October 1995-May 1996) were followed until the date of first cancer diagnosis, death, or end of follow-up (December 31, 2018).
